In this environment, how can we promote the right employees and how do we hire the best canidates when everyone appears to be perfect? Imagine this: You’re hiring a financial analyst and give two finalists the same AI-generated acquisition memo. It reads beautifully and recommends buying a company at what looks like a reasonable price. There’s one problem. The model counted the same revenue twice. One candidate improves the slides. The other asks for the source data, spots the error and changes the recommendation. If I’d asked for a polished take-home assignment and used AI to grade it, I might have hired the better slide editor. AI has become a significant part of how people apply for jobs and how they do that work. Using AI to police that behavior is a losing game. Employers have more to gain by making AI use visible and designing hiring and performance reviews around what people do with it. The better AI gets at writing résumés, the less a perfect match tells you Indeed illustrates both sides of the hiring loop. Its Career Scout offers job seekers résumé help, while its employer tools help review applications against hiring criteria. Both can save time, and résumé assistance can help a qualified applicant explain experience they’ve struggled to put into words. But it can also make two very different candidates look equally well-suited for a role on paper. An AI detector adds another score without answering the question the employer cares about: Could this person do the job? I’d use AI to help the recruiter prepare a better follow-up. If someone says they led an integration, ask them to walk through a decision they made when two teams disagreed. The résumé gets you to the question. The answer gives you something to evaluate. Giving everyone the same AI can make individual judgment easier to see CoderPad offers an interview environment where candidates use AI on realistic tasks while interviewers watch how they prompt, evaluate and revise the output. That gives employers a practical way to observe a skill candidates will increasingly need on the job. I’d give every finalist the same flawed acquisition memo, the same source documents and access to the same AI tools. Then I’d ask what they would verify before sending the memo to a client. One might catch the double-counted revenue. Another might go further and work out whether the corrected numbers change the price we should offer. The most revealing moment may come when the tool confidently insists its original calculation was right. What does the candidate do then? Performance reviews should give people credit for what they catch Lattice lets managers use AI to draft reviews from goals, feedback and meeting notes. Synq, formerly Gloat , says its software can build and run a review cycle from a plain-English instruction. These tools make it easier to collect and summarize evidence. That makes the choice of what to collect more consequential. For a few years, founders might be enamoured of silly monikers, made-up words, and creative misspellings . Then the pendulum swings, and startups defer to simple names that describe what they actually do. So where are we now? Probably somewhere in the middle. Per a Crunchbase analysis of startups 1 founded in the past three years, companies attracting investor interest are largely opting for names that are both distinctive and vague. It’s a preference that reflects this era of fast-evolving AI, in which founders want room to adapt. Examples of this stylistic direction abound among the most heavily funded newer startups. There’s Also , which is of course a micromobility spin-out. Perplexity is a genAI company although you couldn’t tell that by its name. And then there’s Sunday , which makes household robots, in case that wasn’t clear from the name. “Reality is a lot of these companies, in seven or eight years they’ve done at least one or two major pivots,” Athol Foden , who runs the naming consultancy Brighter Naming , told us. That makes it logical to pick a name that can still work afterward. Running out of names When startups do make inventive picks, it’s often out of necessity rather than preference. “We’re running out of words. Everything is trademarked multiple times over,” said Bruno Benedini , co-founder of branding consultancy Taillight . “So we have to look for something unexpected. Given that reality, Benedini is always on the lookout for startups that exemplify the element of surprise. One standout is Hugging Face , the AI model sharing and development platform, which Nvidia agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September. It didn’t succeed just because of its strange name, obviously, but it didn’t hurt. Another more recent upstart that caught his attention is Flapping Airplanes , an AI research lab that raised a $1 billion Series A last month. “It’s super playful, but you remember it, and you have this visual,” he said. Plus, it’s not the kind of name one’s lawyer finds is already taken by a competitor. Building and industry The AI boom is also often characterized as a period in which companies are building the foundational layer of a technology that will fundamentally transform our lives for decades to come. Given this mindset, it’s perhaps predictable that we’re seeing a plethora of names with themes tied to building and industry. Foden points to Databricks as one of the more longstanding representatives of this naming approach. Its brand evokes the notion of digital data as one small component of a massive building endeavor. But newer upstarts are onto this trend as well. There’s an abundance of recently founded companies with “foundation” in their name, for instance, including Foundation Health , Foundation Industries , Foundational Industries , Foundational and Foundation . Another recent example with an industrial, maker vibe is Blacksmith , a cloud infrastructure startup founded in 2024 that’s pulled in more than $100 million this year. Dating app Rivet looks like a more unusual sector match for an industrial name. The two-year-old startup runs a platform in which volunteer matchmakers pick matches for daters. Nuclear startup Standard Nuclear , meanwhile, reads like a twist on Gilded Age industrial giant Standard Oil.
